analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for small groups of employees to form their own union bargaining units.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 13 Republican senators, was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a 2011 National Labor Relations Board ruling, workers can form a union in a small, self-defined group of employees — like one department or one job classification — if the employer cannot show that group should be merged with a larger unit. That makes organizing easier because a union only has to win over a small group of like-interested coworkers. This bill would repeal that standard and require the Board to use a broader set of factors to draw bargaining units, generally producing larger units that are harder for unions to win. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never advanced [S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing union organizing drives. With larger, harder-to-win bargaining units, fewer organizing campaigns succeed and employers keep more direct control over workplace terms without a union counterpart.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the 2011 Specialty Healthcare standard, under which the Board approves a requested bargaining unit unless the employer shows an 'overwhelming community of interest' with other employees, with a standard requiring only a 'sufficient community of interest' judged by factors such as wages, skills, supervision, and workflow [S2][S3].

Directs the Board to weigh the employer's organizational structure and the risk of proliferating or fragmenting units, which tends to produce larger bargaining units than the micro-units allowed under the current standard [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who want to organize a small group of closely similar jobs. Under a larger-unit requirement, a union would have to win elections among broader groups of employees, some of whom may not support organizing, making campaigns more likely to fail.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employees trying to organize small units

drawbacks.text: Employees in a small, distinct job group — for example a single production classification — would generally have to organize alongside larger groups of coworkers with different wages and concerns, diluting their ability to bargain over their own working conditions [S2][S3].

Supporters argue this is a fair trade: micro-units can split one workplace into several conflicting bargaining units, forcing an employer to negotiate separately with employee groups whose interests overlap, which the bill's 'proliferation or fragmentation' language is designed to prevent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For employers, the bill restores a pre-2011 landscape in which bargaining units are larger and union election wins rarer. For workers, the cost is real: the specific employees most likely to use micro-units — small groups with shared job interests — lose their most practical organizing route. Supporters' concern about fragmented, overlapping units is genuine, but the bill addresses it by making organizing broadly harder, not by drawing a narrower line.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, never got a committee vote or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Introduced May 24, 2017, by Sen. Isakson with 12 Republican cosponsors listed at introduction, including the Senate Majority Leader [S1][S3][S4].
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction; that referral was the bill's last action [S5].
The committee never held a markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill during the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the 2011 micro-unit standard remained in place, so employees organizing small bargaining units and the unions assisting them kept the easier path. Employers who wanted it repealed did not get their change.

for.name: Johnny Isakson
for.role: U.S. Senator from Georgia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate labor committee

sides.party_line_note: All 13 original sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; no vote was ever held, so there is no roll call to measure the split [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill raises the bar for forming small bargaining units, making union election wins less likely and leaving employers without a bargaining counterpart over more of the workforce. Its gain comes directly from workers' reduced ability to organize the specific job groups they work in.

Micro-units were a practical organizing tool for unions targeting small, cohesive employee groups; the bill removes that route. Unions' interest here runs alongside the workers they would help organize.
